planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once seedlings have several true leaves, hardening them off against light frost first.

directions: Winnigstadt is a nineteenth-century German heirloom cabbage prized for its dense, hard, cone-shaped heads that taper to a point rather than forming the rounded or flattened heads typical of most cabbage types. The tight wrapper leaves and firm interior give it good natural resistance to splitting in wet weather and reasonable tolerance of heat, making it a flexible choice for both an early spring crop and a second planting for fall harvest. Its small core and dense texture have long made it a favorite for sauerkraut and slaw, and the compact plants can be set closer together than many large-framed cabbages. Harvest when heads feel solid and firm to the squeeze, cutting before hot weather causes the points to loosen and split.

common_name: Hungry Gap Kale (English Heirloom Overwintering Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow in mid to late summer so plants are well established before winter, since this kale is grown through the cold months for a harvest the following early spring rather than in the same season it is sown.

directions: Hungry Gap takes its name from its traditional role in English kitchen gardens, filling the lean stretch in late winter and early spring when stored roots and autumn crops have run out and new spring vegetables have not yet come in. Sown in summer, plants grow slowly through autumn and stand hardy through winter frosts and snow, resuming active growth as days lengthen to supply a flush of tender leaves and shoots exactly when little else is ready. It is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again crop, with young leaves and emerging flower shoots both harvested before the plant bolts fully to seed in spring. Because it is bred for cold survival rather than fast growth, it rewards patience over a long season rather than quick turnover.

common_name: All Seasons Cabbage (American Heirloom Round-Head Cabbage)

planting.note: Start indoors ahead of the last frost and transplant hardened-off seedlings out as soon as the soil can be worked, or sow a second time in midsummer for an autumn crop.

directions: All Seasons is an old American heirloom cabbage valued for its unusual flexibility, producing good round to slightly flattened heads whether sown as an early spring crop or held back for a summer sowing destined for fall harvest. The heads are solid and medium-sized with a tender crisp texture that holds up reasonably well in storage, and the plants show decent tolerance of both the heat of a late planting and the cool snaps of an early one. Because it performs across a wider planting window than many single-purpose cabbages, it has long been a practical choice for home gardeners wanting one variety to cover more than one slot in the rotation. Harvest heads promptly once firm, since like most round cabbages they can split if left too long in wet conditions.

common_name: Couve Galega (Portuguese Tall Kale for Caldo Verde)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or in a nursery bed and transplant out after the last hard frost, giving plants plenty of room to grow into tall, loose-leaved stalks.

directions: Couve Galega is the traditional tall, non-heading Portuguese kale grown throughout rural Portugal as the authentic base for caldo verde soup, distinct from the cabbage-like tronchuda type sometimes sold under a similar regional name. Plants develop a thick central stalk topped with a rosette of broad, smooth, blue-green leaves that are harvested continuously from the bottom up as the stem lengthens over the season. Leaves are traditionally sliced into very thin ribbons for soup, a technique that works well with the tender, non-waxy texture of young growth. It is a vigorous, long-season plant that keeps producing new leaves for months and tolerates cold reasonably well, though it is usually grown as an annual or short-lived biennial in home gardens rather than kept for multiple years.

common_name: Chou Moellier (French Heirloom Marrow-Stem Fodder Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring and thin to final spacing, allowing a long season of growth before the thick stems and leaves are harvested for winter feed.

directions: Chou Moellier is an old French heirloom fodder kale grown for its massive, pith-filled stem and abundant leaf growth, traditionally chopped and fed to livestock through the winter months. The thick, succulent stalk stores more moisture and nutrients than slimmer kale types, which historically made it valuable in regions where winter forage was scarce, and both the stem and the large leaves are palatable to animals once cut. Plants grow tall and sturdy over a long season, tolerating cold well and standing in the field for a late harvest after other crops are finished. While bred for the farmyard rather than the table, the young leaves are also edible for people and taste similar to other non-heading kales, making it a crop of interest to gardeners curious about historic dual-purpose brassicas.
